newsitem.title: USA: Broin case to proceed despite tobacco pact-lawyers.
newsitem.headline: Broin case to proceed despite tobacco pact-lawyers.

text.p: A landmark class-action lawsuit brought against cigarette makers on behalf of flight attendants will go forward in spite of the sweeping tobacco agreement reached on Friday, attorneys said.

"We will be here Monday trying this case," said Edward Moss, an attorney for Brown & Williamson Tobacco Corp, when asked to comment on the proposed industry settlement on Friday, after jury selection had ended for the day.
Brown & Williamson is a unit of B.A.T Industries Plc.
Stanley Rosenblatt, an attorney for the plaintiffs in the suit, known as Norma Broin vs. Philip Morris Cos Inc, also said he expected the case to continue.

He also said he was outraged by the settlement agreement, which would require tobacco companies to pay $368.5 billion over 25 years to compensate state governments and smokers, and fund programs to help people give up cigarettes.

"The bottom line question is, what do the individuals get? ...very little at all," he said. "The tobacco companies will simply raise their prices and addict the Third World. This is just a conscienceless thing. It doesn't even protect American children."
In the Broin case, Rosenblatt is seeking $5 billion in damages on behalf of thousands of flight attendants who claim they were sickened by breathing secondhand smoke on U.S.-based passenger jets.
Dade County Circuit Judge Robert Kaye, who is presiding over the case, said he only wanted to know how a settlement might affect the Broin case. "That's the trouble. They don't tell us," he said.
Previously, he said he expected to continue the Broin case "until something convinces me otherwise."

The attorneys spoke with reporters after completion of a 12th day of jury selection on Friday. To date, attorneys have selected 75 members of the pool from which a panel of six jurors and an estimated 10 alternates will be chosen. Eventually, 100 people are expected to be in the pool.

Kaye said Friday said he wanted jury selection to be completed before the three-day Independence Day weekend, which begins Friday, July 4. He discussed with attorneys different strategies for speeding the process, including starting to question jurors in groups rather than continuing to call them individually, but made no decision.
Kaye has said he would like two or three days after the pool is completed to gather all of the potential jurors to select the final panel.

It was not immediately clear how the settlement agreement would affect Engle vs. R.J. Reynolds, another class-action suit in the same courthouse for which Rosenblatt and his wife, Susan Rosenblatt, are also representing the plaintiffs.
R.J. Reynolds Tobacco Co, which makes Camel, Salem and Winston cigarettes, is a unit of RJR Nabisco Holdings Corp.
That class action, which seeks damages on behalf of 400,000 to 500,000 sick smokers in Florida, was supposed to come to trial September 8, though a delay had been expected because of the Broin trial.

Dade County Circuit Judge Alan Postman had scheduled an emergency hearing on Monday evening at which Rosenblatt said he would present a motion that the judge declare that a industry settlement would not affect the Engle case.
"We're going to fight that," Stanley Rosenblatt said.
